question.prompt: Which of the following conditions is sufficient to guarantee that integers \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z\) satisfy the equation \[ \begin{aligned} &x(x - y) + y(y - z) \\ &\quad {}+ z(z - x) = 1? \end{aligned} \]

solutions.title: Substitute choice D
solutions.explanation:
Choice D sets two variables equal, making one term vanish and simplifying the other two.

Under this condition, \(z=x\) and \(y=x+1\). Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x(x-y)+y(y-z)+z(z-x)
&=x(-1)+(x+1)(1)+x(0)\\
&=-x+x+1\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This calculation holds for every integer \(x\), so the condition always guarantees the equation. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Rewrite as squared differences
solutions.explanation:
The products can be combined into squared differences, which makes the integer restriction useful.

Write
\[
F=x(x-y)+y(y-z)+z(z-x).
\]
Expanding the squares shows that
\[
2F=(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2.
\]
Thus \(F=1\) exactly when the three squares sum to \(2\). Because the differences are integers, each square must be \(0\) or \(1\), and exactly two must be \(1\). This means that two variables are equal and the third differs from them by \(1\).

Choice D gives precisely this pattern: \(x=z\) and \(y=x+1\). Its differences are
\[
x-y=-1,\qquad y-z=1,\qquad z-x=0,
\]
so \(2F=1+1+0=2\), giving \(F=1\). Hence the answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
